title: Oobah Butler Can Sell You Anything—If You’re a Rich Idiot
gist: Wired profile of documentarian Oobah Butler and his HBO series Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow, where he runs fake ventures (children's-tears serum, smoke-tainted wine, a fake AI dating app) to expose weakly regulated industries and gullible elites. Butler argues Big Tech runs on speculative utopian promises used to pump stock prices.

insights.claim: Documentarian Oobah Butler argues Big Tech is built on speculative promises of utopia rather than reality, with tech CEOs overpromising 10-year capabilities to pump their stock prices.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: A cultural signal of rising skepticism toward narrative-driven tech valuations; watch for reputational drag on hype-heavy CEOs.
insights.quote: Tech CEOs constantly coming out and lying about what they’ll be able to do in 10 years to shit-coin their stock price
insights.locator: These days, many of Butler’s stunts

insights.claim: Oobah Butler describes the technology sector as "riddled with inauthenticity," and says many of his stunts now directly or indirectly target Big Tech.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Mainstream satire (HBO) increasingly frames tech as hype; a sentiment headwind for consumer-facing AI branding.
insights.locator: These days, many of Butler’s stunts

insights.claim: In his HBO series, Oobah Butler launched a fake AI dating company called Sole that claimed to match users with a chatbot but actually paired them with other humans, premised on people trusting technology more than conversation with each other.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Illustrates how the 'AI' label alone can confer trust and demand, a dynamic that inflates AI-washing in consumer apps.
insights.quote: The idea was that people trust in the technology more than a conversation with one another
insights.locator: In another episode, Butler starts an AI dating company

insights.claim: Oobah Butler's HBO show depicts him launching a wellness brand selling children's tears as a skin serum, using the stunt to expose the poorly regulated nature of the skin care and supplements industry.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Highlights regulatory laxity in beauty/supplements; a potential reputational or regulatory-risk vector for wellness brands.
insights.quote: a gold rush of bullshit. And I want in.

insights.claim: Former Theranos chief creative officer Patrick O’Neill agreed on camera to advise Butler's fake children's-tears serum brand, suggesting a tear-shaped bottle and the exotic-sounding name Lacrimé to differentiate it from mass brands like Johnson and Johnson.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Shows how mystique-driven marketing playbooks from failed startups remain for hire; treat premium 'exotic' wellness branding skeptically.
insights.quote: It makes it feel exotic and not necessarily something you’d see from Johnson and Johnson
insights.locator: After briefly expressing hesitancy around the ethical sourcing

insights.claim: Butler got New York Times wine critic Eric Asimov to say "I have no complaints" about a smoke-tainted wine brand called Fumare by presenting it as Barolo, then printed that endorsement on the label.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Expert endorsements in luxury goods can be context-driven and gamed; premium pricing often rests on fragile signaling.
insights.locator: Though he may not have firsthand experiences

insights.claim: Butler's satire consistently targets the rich and powerful and the systems that let them prevail, and he says he simply copies real bad actors: 'monkey see, monkey do.'
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
insights.so_what: Each stunt maps onto a real industry abuse, making the show a rough map of sectors with credibility or governance gaps.
insights.quote: I just find these bad actors and copy them.

insights.claim: Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow, launching on HBO November 22, has five episodes covering wellness, wine, dating, music, and a finale, mostly shot by Butler and a couple of collaborators within eight months.
insights.speaker: Manisha Krishnan
entities: Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow
insights.so_what: Premium networks are buying DIY creator-style formats with tiny crews, a low-cost content model for streamers.
insights.quote: One of the episodes was basically me and me in my bedroom
insights.locator: Despite having the backing of HBO
